catalog_quote: 3.1.3 WORD STRESS. The common stress pattern of monomorphemic words of more than one syllable is S.s.S.s (primary stress.nonstress.secondary stress.nonstress) (Sayers 1970a:17ff.) ... If a vowel other than /a/ occurs in what would normally be a nonstress position, it will receive secondary stress ... There are a few forms (about twenty) where the vowel /a/ occurring in a nonstress position receives secondary stress. It seems possible that these words were historically compounds ... There are another twenty forms recorded which have primary stress occurring on other than the first syllable. Some of these are onomatopoeic words or exclamations. sweep_summary: Wik-Mungkan (wikm1247) is in the catalog as fixed-unreviewed (initial primary, alternating secondary, weight-blind) on Kilham 1977 PL B-52 sec 3.1.3, a relay of the lost Sayers 1970a mimeo. Four title hits: (1) Sayers 1976a PL A-42 (held, sealang CC BY-SA) is first-hand and confirms on p.32 ('Normal Rhythm': first syllable stressed, strict alternation; affix classes override, p.33) though Part I is about intonation/clause stress and the Word/Foot Part II was never published; (2) Moore-Cantwell 2016 is an English-stress dissertation attached to Wik-Mungkan by a Glottolog machine mis-assignment (record says so) -- drop from the bibliography; (3) Sayers 1977 'Prosodies in some Aboriginal languages' (SIL PNG Workpapers 20, Iwaidja + Wik-Munkan) not obtainable (sil.org 403, SIL-PNG mirror lacks it, archive.org lacks vol. 20), content unknown, medium priority; (4) Sayers 1976b in Sutton (ed.) Languages of Cape York, pp.284-298, is per Ray 2021 pp.27/82 the published first-hand source that Kilham 1977 and Kilham et al. 1986 summarize, and Ray says its morpheme/word-level stress aligns with initial primary + alternating secondary; only search-only at HathiTrust (record 000126852) and lending-only at archive.org -- high priority for a library scan. Best statement read: Ray 2021 (Monash PhD, open), sec 2.4.5 pp.38-39 and 2.6.1 pp.58-61, with acoustic support, which should become the (co-)deciding modern source; coding unchanged. Nothing found contradicts the catalog.org/aiatsis/hathitrust/scholarworks 403.

new_statements.reading: Modern reference grammar, first-hand corpus analysis with four acoustic correlates (duration, F0, intensity, formants) on archival and 2015 recordings: primary stress on the first syllable, secondary on odd syllables (S.s.S.s), even syllables unstressed; reduplicated prefixes unstressed (primary on the stem); allative -ak attracts stress in even positions (supported), future vs past person suffixes differ by stress alone (partial support); two small classes (kuchek 'head', paththam 'really') take secondary stress on syllable 2 with primary still initial. Weight-blind, fixed initial; exceptions a small listed/morphological set. This confirms the catalog's classification (fixed-unreviewed, initial primary, alternating secondary) and states it more explicitly and with instrumental support than Kilham 1977's relay of the lost Sayers 1970a mimeo; note Ray treats kuchek as initial-primary + second-syllable secondary, whereas Kilham 1977 ex.11 lists it under non-initial primary, which narrows the exception set. Among the four title-hit items themselves, the best first-hand statement read is Sayers 1976a PL A-42 p.32 ('the first syllable is stressed and there is one and only one unstressed syllable between each successive stressed syllable'), which also confirms.

sources.quote: While there are many contrastive stress patterns for Wik-Munkan words, strong structural pressure is exerted by the pattern which I have called Normal Rhythm. This same pattern is described by Dixon (1972:274) for Dyirbal words as the 'preferred' stress pattern. In both languages the first syllable is stressed and there is one and only one unstressed syllable between each successive stressed syllable. [p.33:] ... the pressure of certain affix classes overrides Normal Rhythm. ... Part II, which is to follow, covers the following levels of the phonological hierarchy: the Word, the Foot, the Syllable and the Phoneme.
sources.locator: p.32 (Introduction) and p.33; symbol list sec 3.2 p.~65 marks 'primary word stress' / 'secondary word stress'
sources.note: First-hand (SIL fieldworker, Aurukun 1962-73). Part I treats intonation, clause- and sentence-stress (26 contrastive intonation patterns; clause-stress placement 'phonologically unpredictable and therefore contrastive' but grammatically predictable, p.34); word stress is stated only in the orientation: 'Normal Rhythm' = first syllable stressed, strict alternation (S.s.S.s), overridden by certain affix classes (tense contrasts 'shown only by stress distinctions', p.33).
